content.title: The best time to visit Philadelphia
content.text: By Lindsay CohnJan 30, 2026 • 4 minutes readTaking photos at Love Park, Philadelphia.Image: Maxx882/TripadvisorBefore moving to Philadelphia, I had only visited a handful of times. There was a particularly warm day with my nieces playing on the nets in the waterfront district, a visit to the Rodin Museum with my dad, and a Phillies game. Having lived in the City of Brotherly Love for just over two years, I’ve had the chance to experience it in every season. I’ve admired the crunching leaves in the fall, had a short-lived snowball fight in the winter, glimpsed cherry blossoms in the spring, and sweated it out in the summer. Philadelphians agree on many things: cheesesteaks should be kept simple, Philadelphia is the real birthplace of America (not Boston), and “Go Birds!” works in nearly every conversational context. But the best time to visit is less cut and dry—and that’s because each period offers something unique. Whether you’re plotting a trip to celebrate the United States' Semiquincentennial (250th anniversary) or are just coming to the most exciting food city in the country to eat (yes, I’m biased…but also correct), use these helpful insights on the best times of year to visit to plan the perfect trip.For the best weather: spring and fallRow homes amid cherry blossoms in Philadelphia.Image: Jon Lovette/Getty ImagesThe best weather months are spring (April to May) and fall (September to November). Visitors can expect pleasant temperatures for hitting the many parks and taking historic walking tours. On a particularly nice day, you might even be able to experience Philadelphia’s terrific al fresco dining scene. Cherry blossoms pop up around the city in the spring, and the Japan America Society of Greater Philadelphia hosts the annual cherry blossom festival in West Fairmount Park on the first weekend of April. In the summer, it tends to be very hot and humid, with daytime temperatures in the high 80s. While it’s not as soupy as say Miami or Charleston, travelers will likely want to keep outdoor daytime activities to waterfront pastimes such as strolls along the Schuylkill River or seek out shade at one of the leafy parks. Winter temperatures are mild. While travelers are still at the mercy of frosty temps and the occasional snow squall, it’s more likely you’ll just need to bundle up a bit more. And with so many fantastic indoor attractions, from museums to historic landmarks, it’s not hard to fill an itinerary. For the lowest prices: winterSandwiches at Reading Terminal Market.Image: aLonglunch/TripadvisorWinter is typically the time of year when hotel prices and airfare are at their lowest—the one exception to this rule is the holiday season. Philadelphia gets in the holiday spirit with an open-air Christmas market in JFK Plaza (Love Park) and City Hall's plaza, which also hosts a skating rink. Outside of that period, it’s a bit quieter. That makes it the perfect time to eat your way through Reading Terminal Market, snag a reservation at one of Philadelphia’s best restaurants, and hit the many museums. For historic walking tours: springGuide on the Revolution and the Founders History Tour of Philadelphia.Image: rpmanville/TripadvisorPhiladelphia is also the birthplace of the United States, and there are numerous preserved landmarks dating back to the Revolutionary period. Many of the must-see sites are congregated in Old City, interspersed with cobbled streets and brick row homes. It’s one of the most beautiful and busy parts of the city for sightseeing—made even prettier by the cherry blossoms in the spring. It’s not just the pretty pink buds that make April and May the best time for a historic walking tour. The mild, usually sunny weather makes it pleasant for an extended stroll outside.While you can certainly plod along at your own pace and read the various placards, booking a guided tour allows you to see these historic sights from the perspective of a historian with deep knowledge of the subject and a history degree. The Revolution and the Founders: History Tour of Philadelphia is one of the most popular and well-reviewed tours in the city, taking visitors (or locals who want to learn more about our nation's founding) on a two-hour tour of key sights, including Independence Hall, where the Declaration of Independence and U.S. Constitution were drafted and signed, and the Liberty Bell. With kids: spring and fallChild posing for a photo at the Philadelphia Zoo.Image: christellsc/TripadvisorOne of the things that’s so great about Philadelphia is that indoor and outdoor activities abound for children. If you’re looking to hit the parks and riverfront, come spring (March to May) and fall (September to November). Should you plan to dedicate much of your time to the museums, summer (June to August) or even winter (December to February) work, too. Sister Cities Park, Smith Memorial Playground, and Schuylkill River Park are some of the top picks for families looking to get some fresh air and let little ones engage in some play. Sister Cities Park has a water feature in the warmer months, while Smith Memorial Playground boasts the best play setups in Philadelphia, with age-appropriate and giant slides to race down in potato sacks. Wissahickon Valley Park has over 50 miles of trails, with plenty of short scenic walks for tots and longer paths for teens and tweens. There are picnic areas and streams for trout fishing as well. While it’s lovely in the spring, it’s especially pretty in the fall with the color-changing leaves. The Philadelphia Zoo, America’s oldest zoo, is another great place to go when the weather is nice—it’s home to 1,900 rare and endangered animals, plus a farm feeding area, a playground, a carousel, and a mini train. For those who make a visit in the winter months, Philadelphia has a deep well of museums for year-round education and entertainment, many of which are situated around the Benjamin Franklin Parkway, part of Logan Square, often referred to as "Museum Mile.” First up, a favorite of my kids: The Franklin Institute. This world-class science museum offers exhibits where kids can learn about the human body, see what it would be like to jump without gravity, whirl marbles into a black hole in space, learn how to fold and fly paper airplanes, sit inside an old fighter jet in the aviation section, and race against Gritty at the sport exercise area on the top floor. There’s also an excellent planetarium. Next up, the Academy of Natural Sciences of Drexel University—or, as my kids like to call it, “the dinosaur museum”—is a wonderful place to encourage children’s passion for animals, past and present. (Don’t miss the mock dig for budding paleontologists.) The Please Touch Museum is a sure bet to pass a few hours of indoor time while kids play chef at the 3,650-square-foot grocery and kitchen exhibit and let imagination run wild at the lower-level Fairytale Garden.
